papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavioral and representational knowledge from teacher models. The field has diversified from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes internal-representation alignment, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, addressing teacher–student gaps, and combining distillation with complementary compression strategies when data or latency constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, deployable students. Its effectiveness depends on what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, feature distributions) and how the teacher signals are adapted to student capacity and task constraints. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox: select and combine response-, feature-, and curriculum-based distillation techniques, adopt multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning or progressive replacement) when latency, data, or robustness constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the last decade KD diversified from simple soft-label transfer into many variants that match logits, internal representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics, and that interact with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning and progressive module replacement. Practical deployment benefits most from hybrid, task-aware strategies that select what to transfer, adapt the teacher-student relationship, and combine distillation with pruning or architectural replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Empirical Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a broad set of techniques that include representation-level matching, multi- and online-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning and progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, natural language understanding, summarization, machine translation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD can substantially close the gap between compact students and their larger teachers, but success depends on matching the form and amount of transferred knowledge to student capacity, task demands, and data/latency/robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a simple teacher-to-student soft-label transfer into a rich family of methods that target robustness, internal representation alignment, task-specific selection of signals, and efficient compression pipelines. Across vision, language, and sequence generation tasks, distillation enables compact models to retain or approach the performance of large models while enabling practical latency and memory benefits. Effective distillation designs combine multiple signals (logits, hidden states, feature correlations), adapt the teacher-student relationship during training, and can be integrated with pruning or module-replacement strategies to achieve strong trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring behavior and internal structure. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a toolbox of methods—logit/soft-label transfer, alignment of intermediate and attention representations, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online/evolving and multi-teacher schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, engineering teacher–student relationships, and integrating complementary compression techniques when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and natural language processing. KD encompasses transferring final outputs (soft logits), intermediate and attention representations, and aspects of training dynamics, and is most effective when chosen and combined with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) to match student capacity and task constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its practical success depends on teacher–student matching, data availability, and attention to robustness; hybrid, task-aware pipelines and careful teacher engineering are therefore recommended.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond soft‑target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes logits and soft-label matching, intermediate-representation and attention/feature matching, inter-channel and feature-correlation objectives, adversarial and contrastive losses, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self- and meta-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results show KD routinely improves compact-model performance across vision, language, ranking, generation, and reinforcement learning when its components are chosen to match student capacity, task constraints, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing data and compute costs of distillation, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its many variants—logit transfer, intermediate-representation matching, attention- and feature-based matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- or online-teachers, and curriculum-style schedules—provide different trade-offs among accuracy, latency, robustness, and data requirements. Rather than a single recipe, effective compression arises from selecting and combining KD methods to match student capacity and task constraints, often in combination with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or module replacement.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategies for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, but its success hinges on matching the distillation strategy to task demands, student capacity, and data constraints. Rather than a single recipe, KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox combining soft-labels, internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, layer-wise filtering, adversarial objectives, and pruning or module-replacement where appropriate. When chosen and combined thoughtfully—exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and using task-aware selection—KD yields compact models that retain high performance, robustness, and practical latency gains.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that success depends less on a single canonical loss and more on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and adapted to the student and the target task. Best results arise when distillation methods (1) expose informative internal representations rather than only final logits, (2) adapt or curate teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and (3) combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement). When applied with attention to these aspects, distillation yields compact models that maintain high accuracy, can inherit robustness, and scale to practical inference budgets.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the state of knowledge distillation (KD) and its role in model compression for deep learning and NLP. It surveys what is transferred from teachers to students (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive/evolving schemes), the principal mechanisms by which distillation benefits students (label smoothing, reduced data complexity, representation shaping, and gradient/decision-boundary effects), common applications across NLP tasks, empirical practicalities and trade-offs (teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness transfer, and compute/latency constraints), and recommended task-aware, hybrid practices that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. The synthesis also highlights recurring open challenges such as reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant teacher signals for a given student capacity, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and How to Use It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible route to producing compact, high-performance models for deep learning and NLP. When matched to task requirements and student capacity and when combined with complementary compression strategies, distillation routinely yields models that approach the accuracy of large teachers while delivering meaningful latency and memory gains. However, distillation is not universally superior: its benefits depend on what form of knowledge is transferred, the availability and complexity of training data, and the desired properties (e.g., robustness, latency). I argue that distillation should be treated as an indispensable component of a compression toolbox — applied with representation-level signals, teacher-aware adaptations, and hybridization with pruning or progressive replacement when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that, when designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and combined with complementary compression techniques, routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. Its mechanisms include soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation matching, teacher scheduling (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), and adversarial or contrastive objectives. Practical success requires adapting teacher signals to task and data constraints and recognizing limitations such as teacher–student capacity gaps, data requirements, and robustness transfer challenges.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a configurable toolbox of techniques chosen to match student capacity, task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical compression combines forms of transferred knowledge (logits, internal representations, attention/feature structure), teacher engineering (confidence- or task-aware weighting, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules), adversarial/robustness-aware objectives, and complementary compression such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. The recommended approach is to select and combine distillation components according to the specific application rather than relying on one canonical loss.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Tradeoffs, and a Practical Toolbox
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. A broad family of KD methods—logit-based soft targets, internal representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher optimization (meta or student-friendly), multi-teacher weighting, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has emerged to address capacity gaps, task specificity, robustness, and data availability. Effective compression in practice requires choosing and often combining methods according to the target task, student capacity, and data constraints: internal- and layer-wise matching improves task transfer; confidence- and task-aware weighting mitigates low-quality supervision; adversarial and robust distillation protect model reliability; and structured pruning can match distillation in latency-sensitive scenarios. The most reliable strategy is a toolbox approach that aligns the distillation objective with the student’s capacity and the application constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely used family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD is best understood as a design space: practitioners transfer final soft-labels, intermediate representations, attention or feature statistics, and even training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, and self-distillation regimes; and they combine distillation with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning and progressive module replacement. KD works via multiple mechanisms (regularization-like effects, richer per-instance signals, representation shaping, and improved optimization trajectories) and is most effective when tailored to student capacity, task specifics, and data availability. Hybrid, task-aware pipelines that select what information to transfer, adapt teacher signals, and integrate pruning or module replacement are the most reliable practical path. Important limitations remain: teacher–student capacity gaps, dependence on unlabeled data in some regimes, partial transfer of robustness, and the need for principled selection of task-relevant signals to copy or omit.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a diverse and practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large models (teachers) to smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency while preserving performance. The literature spans soft-target (logit) transfer, internal- and layer-wise representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online/evolving teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical results across vision and a wide range of NLP tasks (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, dense retrieval) show that no single recipe suffices: success depends on the choice of distilled signal, teacher–student capacity gap, task complexity, and data availability. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a toolbox of complementary methods whose components should be selected and combined according to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring behavior and internal structure. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a toolbox of methods—logit/soft-label transfer, alignment of intermediate and attention representations, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online/evolving and multi-teacher schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, engineering teacher–student relationships, and integrating complementary compression techniques when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller students to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Research has mapped multiple mechanisms by which KD helps (regularization, label-structure transfer, representation shaping, and per-instance gradient reweighting) and developed many variants that transfer logits, intermediate features, attention/feature correlations, or decision-boundary signals. KD is commonly combined with structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and task-aware filtering to meet latency and robustness constraints, and contemporary work emphasizes matching distilled information to student capacity and the target task.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, deployable students. Its effectiveness depends on what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, feature distributions) and how the teacher signals are adapted to student capacity and task constraints. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox: select and combine response-, feature-, and curriculum-based distillation techniques, adopt multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning or progressive replacement) when latency, data, or robustness constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label matching into a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and task-aware schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting or selecting teacher signals to be student-friendly, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require it. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, minimizing teacher–student mismatch, and reducing the data and compute overhead of effective distillation.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques aim to transfer performance from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, more efficient models for deployment or specialized use. Approaches span logit-based soft-label distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, teacher design and selection strategies, online/evolutionary teachers, curriculum or route-based supervision, and combinations with pruning and adversarial methods. In NLP, distillation has been adapted to pretrained transformers via progressive module replacement, layer-wise and task-aware filters, and by leveraging distilled data (pseudo-labeling) or parameter shrinking. Trade-offs include reliance on unlabeled data, teacher-student capacity gaps, and robustness concerns; recent work addresses these via teacher adaptation, confidence-weighting, and distillation objectives targeting representation geometry and decision boundaries.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Structured Pruning Learns Compact and Accurate Models
papers_seen.abstract: The growing size of neural language models has led to increased attention in model compression. The two predominant approaches are pruning, which gradually removes weights from a pre-trained model, and distillation, which trains a smaller compact model to match a larger one. Pruning methods can significantly reduce the model size but hardly achieve large speedups as distillation. However, distillation methods require large amounts of unlabeled data and are expensive to train. In this work, we propose a task-specific structured pruning method CoFi (Coarse- and Fine-grained Pruning), which delivers highly parallelizable subnetworks and matches the distillation methods in both accuracy and latency, without resorting to any unlabeled data. Our key insight is to jointly prune coarse-grained (e.g., layers) and fine-grained (e.g., heads and hidden units) modules, which controls the pruning decision of each parameter with masks of different granularity. We also devise a layerwise distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from unpruned to pruned models during optimization. Our experiments on GLUE and SQuAD datasets show that CoFi yields models with over 10x speedups with a small accuracy drop, showing its effectiveness and efficiency compared to previous pruning and distillation approaches.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as an indispensable, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designers choose what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules) as required by deployment constraints, KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to the student and task, guarding against teacher–student mismatches, and addressing limits in robustness transfer and data/compute demands through hybrid and student-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer useful predictive behavior from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) while preserving accuracy and often adding desirable properties such as robustness or task-specific efficiency. A wide range of methods has been developed: soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer- or module-wise compression, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, summarization, and reinforcement learning show that carefully chosen distillation strategies can reclaim much of a teacher's performance in a compact student, but outcomes depend strongly on the choice of distilled signals, the alignment of capacities, teacher selection or adaptation, and task-specific constraints. Recent work also emphasizes robustness transfer, task-aware filtering of teacher signals, and alternatives to distillation such as structured pruning that can match distillation in latency without extra unlabeled data. Remaining challenges include principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer, scaling to diverse prediction tasks, and combining distillation with compression and robustness objectives in a computationally efficient way.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: Essential, Effective, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single soft-label trick into a broad, task-aware toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into compact, deployable students. When matched to student capacity, adapted to task constraints, and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement), KD routinely produces models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness needs. At the same time, KD has limits tied to data requirements, teacher–student capacity gaps, and robustness transfer; practical deployment benefits from hybrid, selective, and teacher-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers
papers_seen.abstract: We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers consistent gains when its objectives and signals (logits, internal representations, attention maps, contrastive or adversarial losses) are matched to student capacity and task constraints and when it is combined with complementary compression strategies such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. However, KD is not universally optimal: careful teacher design, task-aware signal selection, and hybrid pipelines are often required to realize the best latency–accuracy–robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. Practical compression succeeds by (1) exposing and aligning informative internal representations, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task requirements, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. With these design patterns, distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world deployment constraints, though limits remain when data is scarce or teacher–student gaps are large.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques that compress large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD has evolved from soft-label matching into many variants—intermediate-representation alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, curriculum and route-based supervision, online/multi-teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the type of transferred signal to student capacity and task demands, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. When treated as a toolbox—covering soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and integrations with pruning or module replacement—KD reliably reduces model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics, and accounting for data and robustness constraints. KD is indispensable for many practical deployments, but practitioners should combine it with complementary compression strategies and task-aware design to navigate limits posed by capacity gaps, data scarcity, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.
