papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning tasks, KD methods have been extended with architectural, training, and curriculum innovations to address capacity gaps, robustness, and task specificity. Effective deployment of KD requires matching what is distilled (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or structural operators) to the student capacity and the target task; complementary methods such as structured pruning and curriculum-based teacher schedules can further improve trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label (logit) matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher regimes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representational structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching into a configurable toolbox that includes logits matching, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and multi- or online-teacher schedules. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and data availability—and when combined thoughtfully with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on the form of transferred signals, teacher–student gaps, and robustness or data limitations, motivating hybrid, task-aware designs and continued research into teacher adaptation and training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques aim to transfer performance from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, more efficient models for deployment or specialized use. Approaches span logit-based soft-label distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, teacher design and selection strategies, online/evolutionary teachers, curriculum or route-based supervision, and combinations with pruning and adversarial methods. In NLP, distillation has been adapted to pretrained transformers via progressive module replacement, layer-wise and task-aware filters, and by leveraging distilled data (pseudo-labeling) or parameter shrinking. Trade-offs include reliance on unlabeled data, teacher-student capacity gaps, and robustness concerns; recent work addresses these via teacher adaptation, confidence-weighting, and distillation objectives targeting representation geometry and decision boundaries.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a diverse set of approaches that transfer logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics; employ single, multi-, or evolving-teacher schedules; and combine naturally with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When practitioners match what is transferred to student capacity and the target task, distillation commonly yields compact models with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs; remaining challenges include capacity gaps, robustness transfer, data requirements, and selecting task-relevant internal signals.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large pretrained models into smaller, more efficient models by transferring learned knowledge from teacher to student. A rich variety of techniques have been developed: matching soft targets, aligning intermediate and internal representations, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. These techniques have been applied across vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning tasks, and have been analyzed to explain when and why distillation helps. Empirical work shows distillation can reduce model size and preserve or improve performance, but effectiveness depends on the choice of teacher, the form of transferred knowledge, data complexity, and task-specific design choices.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Towards Effective and Robust Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Distillation-Centric Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically powerful tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students. I argue that the most reliable path to high-quality compressed models in both vision and NLP is a hybrid approach that (1) emphasizes internal-representation and layer-wise distillation for transferring structured task-relevant knowledge, (2) uses task-aware selection and teacher-selection strategies to reduce irrelevant signal, (3) integrates adversarial and robustness-aware techniques when robustness matters, and (4) combines distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement when latency and memory constraints dominate. This position synthesizes empirical and theoretical findings across distillation, multi-teacher strategies, robustness, and pruning to recommend practical design patterns for model compression.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designed to match what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention or feature correlations) and how teachers and students are coupled (teacher engineering, online or multi-teacher schemes, curriculum or route-based schedules), KD routinely produces compact models that approach the performance of large teachers while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness requirements. The most reliable practice combines representation-focused distillation with teacher adaptation and, when necessary, complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement to address severe latency or data constraints.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavioral and representational knowledge from teacher models. The field has diversified from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes internal-representation alignment, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, addressing teacher–student gaps, and combining distillation with complementary compression strategies when data or latency constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring behavioral and representational information from large teacher models to smaller student models so they meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, robustness) while preserving performance. KD has grown from soft-target matching into a rich, task-aware toolbox that includes logits and intermediate-representation matching, attention and feature-correlation transfer, self- and multi-teacher schemes, curriculum/meta-learning schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Key practical challenges include matching transferred signals to student capacity, bridging teacher–student gaps, managing data and robustness constraints, and choosing complementary compression steps for target deployment.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designed to match what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), how teachers and students are coupled (teacher engineering, online or multi-teacher schemes, curriculum or route-based schedules), and when combined with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement), KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness requirements. However, the practical success of KD depends on matching transfer signals to student capacity and task demands, managing teacher–student capacity gaps, and addressing data and robustness constraints; in some settings, alternative or hybrid compression strategies may be preferable.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, effective distillation is a design space of complementary techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher design, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or progressive module replacement. When chosen and combined with attention to teacher–student capacity, task characteristics, and data availability, distillation reliably yields compact models that preserve accuracy and can transfer robustness; when misapplied it can be outperformed by simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or structured pruning strategies. I argue that the best practical posture is to treat distillation as a task-aware hybrid toolbox: prioritize representation-level transfer and teacher engineering, use confidence- or task-aware weighting for multiple signals, integrate robustness-aware objectives when needed, and combine distillation with pruning or module replacement when latency/memory constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a diverse and practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large models (teachers) to smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency while preserving performance. The literature spans soft-target (logit) transfer, internal- and layer-wise representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online/evolving teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical results across vision and a wide range of NLP tasks (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, dense retrieval) show that no single recipe suffices: success depends on the choice of distilled signal, teacher–student capacity gap, task complexity, and data availability. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a toolbox of complementary methods whose components should be selected and combined according to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Evolving, and Complementary to Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into compact students suitable for deployment. A broad and active literature has developed specialized KD variants that address teacher selection, internal representation transfer, robustness, task-specific filtering, online and ensemble distillation, and model-structure-aware compression. While KD is highly effective across vision and NLP tasks, recent work shows that pruning and module-replacement strategies can be competitive or complementary, particularly when unlabeled data or heavy distillation training is impractical. Best practice is to treat distillation as a toolbox: select methods that reduce teacher-student capacity gap, transfer internal representations and task-relevant features, and incorporate confidence or robustness objectives when needed, while considering pruning or progressive replacement when latency or data constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practically central approach for producing compact neural models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher training, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals and teacher strategies to student capacity, task requirements, and available data; when designed carefully, KD enables substantial latency and memory gains while retaining strong accuracy across vision, NLP, ranking, retrieval, and reinforcement-learning tasks.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The field offers a broad, configurable toolkit—ranging from soft-target matching to layer-wise representation alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning—to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints across vision and NLP applications. Practical success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, task characteristics, and available data.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises a toolbox of techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, engineering teacher supervision to be student-friendly, and choosing complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require them. While KD is often indispensable for deployment, alternative or hybrid strategies (structured pruning, shrink-and-fine-tune) can be competitive in constrained regimes.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its strengths arise from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, internal representation transfer, teacher engineering, and supervised schedules), and the most reliable practical strategies treat KD as a configurable toolbox that is combined with pruning or module replacement when deployment constraints demand it. Practitioners obtain the best trade-offs by matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics to the task, and using hybrid pipelines tailored to data, latency, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: The Continuing Value of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (and When Hybrids Are Better)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained environments. KD works through multiple mechanisms — smoothing/regularization, transfer of structured class- and instance-level information, and alignment of internal representations — and can be improved by task-aware, teacher-aware, and curriculum-inspired strategies. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: structured pruning and module-replacement methods can match or exceed KD under certain data- or compute-constrained regimes, and simple strategies like shrink-and-fine-tune sometimes outperform explicit distillation for particular pre-trained NLP models and datasets. Best outcomes typically come from principled combinations: selecting or training student-friendly teachers, matching intermediate representations selectively, using task-aware filters, and combining KD with pruning or specialized distillation objectives tailored to the model and task.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models or produce compact subnetworks via pruning and module replacement. The literature has grown into a design space of methods that transfer final outputs (soft logits), internal representations (feature maps, attention, layer activations), or training dynamics (curricula, evolving teachers), and which operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical and analytical work shows that success depends on matching the distilled information to student capacity and task demands, combining complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning or module replacement) when appropriate, and addressing practical constraints such as unlabeled-data needs, robustness transfer, and optimization stability. Effective distillation usually involves exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to the student, and selecting task-relevant knowledge rather than naively copying all teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP the field has moved beyond single-loss soft-target matching to a rich set of transferable signals and training schedules that include logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, confidence-aware weighting, multi- or online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred knowledge to student capacity and task constraints, adaptively shaping teacher signals, and—when needed—integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, dealing with teacher–student capacity gaps, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely used family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD is best understood as a design space: practitioners transfer final soft-labels, intermediate representations, attention or feature statistics, and even training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, and self-distillation regimes; and they combine distillation with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning and progressive module replacement. KD works via multiple mechanisms (regularization-like effects, richer per-instance signals, representation shaping, and improved optimization trajectories) and is most effective when tailored to student capacity, task specifics, and data availability. Hybrid, task-aware pipelines that select what information to transfer, adapt teacher signals, and integrate pruning or module replacement are the most reliable practical path. Important limitations remain: teacher–student capacity gaps, dependence on unlabeled data in some regimes, partial transfer of robustness, and the need for principled selection of task-relevant signals to copy or omit.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. KD succeeds not because it is a single fixed recipe but because it is a design space: practitioners can choose what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, feature correlations, or decision-boundary information), how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and whether to combine distillation with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. KD yields consistent gains when matched to task constraints and student capacity, but it has limits — notably sensitivity to teacher–student gaps, data complexity, and some robustness-transfer failures — that motivate hybrid, task-aware strategies and careful teacher engineering.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its effectiveness stems from several complementary mechanisms—soft-target supervision, alignment of intermediate representations, and shaping of training dynamics—and from its flexibility to be combined with methods such as progressive module replacement and structured pruning. While distillation often delivers strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, realizing those gains requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to adapt the teacher signal to student capacity, and when to hybridize distillation with other compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox that, when matched to student capacity and combined with complementary compression strategies, produces compact models that approach the performance of large teachers while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective use of distillation emphasizes representation-level signals, teacher adaptation, and selective or progressive transfer of modules; its limits arise from teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute availability, and the choice of which form of knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavioral and representational knowledge from teacher models. The field has diversified from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes internal-representation alignment, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, addressing teacher–student gaps, and combining distillation with complementary compression strategies when data or latency constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and versatile approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students in vision and NLP. KD is best treated as a configurable, task-aware toolbox that transfers logits, internal representations, attention or feature structure, and can be combined with teacher engineering, multi-teacher or online schedules, adversarial/contrastive objectives, and complementary compression such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness; however, limits remain related to teacher–student capacity gaps, data requirements, and reliable robustness transfer. Practical success comes from task-aware selection of signals, adaptive teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that incorporate pruning or module replacement when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, deployable students. Its effectiveness depends on what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, feature distributions) and how the teacher signals are adapted to student capacity and task constraints. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox: select and combine response-, feature-, and curriculum-based distillation techniques, adopt multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning or progressive replacement) when latency, data, or robustness constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.
