papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. KD succeeds not because it is a single fixed recipe but because it is a design space: practitioners can choose what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, feature correlations, or decision-boundary information), how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and whether to combine distillation with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. KD yields consistent gains when matched to task constraints and student capacity, but it has limits — notably sensitivity to teacher–student gaps, data complexity, and some robustness-transfer failures — that motivate hybrid, task-aware strategies and careful teacher engineering.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Work across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding shows KD variants — from soft-label matching to internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, adversarial and curriculum-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines combining pruning or module replacement — routinely recover much of teacher performance when the distillation strategy is matched to task demands and student capacity. Important limitations remain: sensitivity to teacher–student capacity gaps, reliance on unlabeled data and heavy distillation compute in some pipelines, and uneven transfer of robustness, motivating continued research into targeted transfer signals and efficient, student-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned teachers, multi-teacher or online schemes), and task-specific constraints. When combined with complementary approaches such as structured pruning or curriculum-style supervision, distillation yields compact models suitable for real-world NLP and vision deployments while enabling trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, and feature correlations, and extend to adversarial, contrastive, curriculum, multi-teacher, and meta-learned strategies. Best practices emphasize selecting which teacher signals to transfer, matching distilled information to student capacity and task needs, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning shows that task-aware, hybrid distillation pipelines typically deliver the most reliable trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a diverse and practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large models (teachers) to smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency while preserving performance. The literature spans soft-target (logit) transfer, internal- and layer-wise representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online/evolving teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical results across vision and a wide range of NLP tasks (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, dense retrieval) show that no single recipe suffices: success depends on the choice of distilled signal, teacher–student capacity gap, task complexity, and data availability. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a toolbox of complementary methods whose components should be selected and combined according to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models or produce compact subnetworks via pruning and module replacement. The literature has grown into a design space of methods that transfer final outputs (soft logits), internal representations (feature maps, attention, layer activations), or training dynamics (curricula, evolving teachers), and which operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical and analytical work shows that success depends on matching the distilled information to student capacity and task demands, combining complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning or module replacement) when appropriate, and addressing practical constraints such as unlabeled-data needs, robustness transfer, and optimization stability. Effective distillation usually involves exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to the student, and selecting task-relevant knowledge rather than naively copying all teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolkit for producing compact models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves student performance by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and training dynamics, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as part of a hybrid compression pipeline—selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when needed.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond soft-label supervision into a design space that includes intermediate-representation matching, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary teachers, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves compact model performance across vision and NLP tasks (including pretrained transformer compression, machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, and continual learning), but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity gap, availability of data, and task-specific constraints. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most usefully viewed not as a single algorithm but as a configurable, task-aware toolbox. When practitioners select what to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits — it depends on data complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the choice of transferred signals — and in some regimes alternative compression strategies can match or exceed distillation unless hybridized thoughtfully.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring useful predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to smaller students. The field encompasses a wide spectrum of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher strategies, and combinations with structured pruning — each suited to different capacity gaps, data regimes, latency constraints, and robustness needs. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation helps by smoothing supervision, reducing data complexity, shaping per-instance gradients and decision boundaries, and providing representational priors that smaller models can exploit. Effective compression typically requires choosing or adapting what is transferred to the student's capacity and the target task, and often benefits from hybrid strategies (e.g., distillation plus pruning or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from training compact students on teacher soft labels to a diverse set of techniques that transfer knowledge via logits, intermediate representations, attention, adversarial objectives, and dynamic teacher-student interactions. Modern work emphasizes transferring internal structure (e.g., feature maps, layer representations, inter-channel correlations), leveraging multiple or evolving teachers, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement for efficient deployment. Applications range from machine translation and summarization to ranking, detection, reinforcement learning, and robustness, and recent advances show task-aware, confidence-weighted, and adversarial approaches often outperform vanilla logit-matching.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: An Argument for Its Central Role in Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students when treated as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox. By selecting and combining signals (soft outputs, internal representations, attention/feature maps), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and integrating distillation with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules), practitioners can achieve strong accuracy–latency–size trade-offs. KD has limits — including teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute needs, and uneven robustness transfer — so it must be applied judiciously and compared or combined with other compression approaches in constrained regimes.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a diverse set of approaches that transfer logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics; employ single, multi-, or evolving-teacher schedules; and combine naturally with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When practitioners match what is transferred to student capacity and the target task, distillation commonly yields compact models with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs; remaining challenges include capacity gaps, robustness transfer, data requirements, and selecting task-relevant internal signals.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer useful predictive behavior from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) while preserving accuracy and often adding desirable properties such as robustness or task-specific efficiency. A wide range of methods has been developed: soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer- or module-wise compression, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, summarization, and reinforcement learning show that carefully chosen distillation strategies can reclaim much of a teacher's performance in a compact student, but outcomes depend strongly on the choice of distilled signals, the alignment of capacities, teacher selection or adaptation, and task-specific constraints. Recent work also emphasizes robustness transfer, task-aware filtering of teacher signals, and alternatives to distillation such as structured pruning that can match distillation in latency without extra unlabeled data. Remaining challenges include principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer, scaling to diverse prediction tasks, and combining distillation with compression and robustness objectives in a computationally efficient way.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring information from a teacher to a smaller student. Methods vary widely: matching output soft-labels, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and contrastive approaches, curriculum and meta-learning strategies, and task-aware layer selection. In NLP, and particularly with large pretrained Transformers, distillation is applied both during pretraining and fine-tuning; alternative compression strategies (e.g., pruning) are often combined with distillation to trade off size, speed, and accuracy. Empirical and theoretical work highlights multiple mechanisms by which distillation helps students, including regularization, reduced data complexity, and per-instance gradient shaping.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a broad design space for transferring predictive behavior from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Methods range from soft-target matching to internal-representation alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or task-aware filtering. Empirical evidence across natural language tasks (classification, summarization, translation, retrieval) and other domains shows that KD can preserve or approach teacher performance while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, data complexity, and task constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: A Distillation-First Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Best results arise from (1) transferring internal, structured representations in addition to logits, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression strategies such as progressive module replacement or structured pruning. This position synthesizes empirical and algorithmic advances to recommend practical design patterns for building compact, robust models for deployment in vision, language, and reinforcement-learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label (logit) matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher regimes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field treats distillation as a toolbox of methods—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, using contrastive/adversarial objectives, and employing multi- or online-teacher schedules—often in hybrid pipelines together with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, choosing suitable teacher schedules, and integrating complementary compression techniques when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Tradeoffs, and a Practical Toolbox
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. A broad family of KD methods—logit-based soft targets, internal representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher optimization (meta or student-friendly), multi-teacher weighting, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has emerged to address capacity gaps, task specificity, robustness, and data availability. Effective compression in practice requires choosing and often combining methods according to the target task, student capacity, and data constraints: internal- and layer-wise matching improves task transfer; confidence- and task-aware weighting mitigates low-quality supervision; adversarial and robust distillation protect model reliability; and structured pruning can match distillation in latency-sensitive scenarios. The most reliable strategy is a toolbox approach that aligns the distillation objective with the student’s capacity and the application constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned teachers, multi-teacher or online schemes), and task-specific constraints. When combined with complementary approaches such as structured pruning or curriculum-style supervision, distillation yields compact models suitable for real-world NLP and vision deployments while enabling trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching into a rich design space that includes logits and temperature tuning, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and progressive module-replacement pipelines. Empirical work across computer vision, language understanding, translation, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD often substantially narrows the performance gap between teacher and student while improving latency and memory usage; however, success depends on matching what and how information is transferred to student capacity, task constraints, and available data. Complementary methods (structured pruning, module replacement, and teacher adaptation) and task-aware choices usually yield the most reliable compression outcomes. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, handling teacher–student capacity gaps, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP

Empirical work shows KD can deliver strong accuracy–latency–memory trade-offs across vision and many NLP tasks, but its success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement). Important open problems include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora or heavy distillation compute.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer useful predictive behavior from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) while preserving accuracy and often adding desirable properties such as robustness or task-specific efficiency. A wide range of methods has been developed: soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer- or module-wise compression, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, summarization, and reinforcement learning show that carefully chosen distillation strategies can reclaim much of a teacher's performance in a compact student, but outcomes depend strongly on the choice of distilled signals, the alignment of capacities, teacher selection or adaptation, and task-specific constraints. Recent work also emphasizes robustness transfer, task-aware filtering of teacher signals, and alternatives to distillation such as structured pruning that can match distillation in latency without extra unlabeled data. Remaining challenges include principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer, scaling to diverse prediction tasks, and combining distillation with compression and robustness objectives in a computationally efficient way.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategies for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, but its success hinges on matching the distillation strategy to task demands, student capacity, and data constraints. Rather than a single recipe, KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox combining soft-labels, internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, layer-wise filtering, adversarial objectives, and pruning or module-replacement where appropriate. When chosen and combined thoughtfully—exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and using task-aware selection—KD yields compact models that retain high performance, robustness, and practical latency gains.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for producing compact, deployable models. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond simple soft-target matching into a diverse set of approaches that transfer outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics; employ single, multi, or evolving teachers; and combine with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and natural language tasks show that, when matched to student capacity, task constraints, and data availability, distillation often yields substantial improvements in accuracy, latency, and memory compared to naive shrink-and-fine-tune baselines. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness and decision-boundary information, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora or heavy distillation compute.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood and applied as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Effective compression requires choosing which signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, decision-boundary cues), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity (including online or evolving teachers and student-friendly teacher training), and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) when deployment constraints demand it. Across vision, NLP, machine translation, and reinforcement learning, this hybrid, capacity-matched approach consistently yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in both vision and natural language processing. The field has expanded well beyond soft-target matching to include representation-level alignment, attention and correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, progressive module replacement, and hybrids that pair distillation with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering. Effective compression is task- and capacity-aware: choosing what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student constraints is key to preserving accuracy, latency, and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.title: Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and How to Use It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible route to producing compact, high-performance models for deep learning and NLP. When matched to task requirements and student capacity and when combined with complementary compression strategies, distillation routinely yields models that approach the accuracy of large teachers while delivering meaningful latency and memory gains. However, distillation is not universally superior: its benefits depend on what form of knowledge is transferred, the availability and complexity of training data, and the desired properties (e.g., robustness, latency). I argue that distillation should be treated as an indispensable component of a compression toolbox — applied with representation-level signals, teacher-aware adaptations, and hybridization with pruning or progressive replacement when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, task-aware design space for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. The field has expanded from soft-label matching to include intermediate-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary and online teachers, and progressive module replacement. KD is most effective when chosen and combined according to task constraints, student capacity, data availability, and goals (latency, memory, or robustness); complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive replacement are often used alongside KD to meet deployment requirements. Empirical work shows that, when applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that recover much of teacher performance while delivering meaningful reductions in parameter count and inference cost, though open challenges remain around teacher–student gaps, robustness transfer, and data-limited regimes.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, Task Considerations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple soft-target matching into a rich set of methods that transfer logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information; use single, multiple, evolving, or learned teachers; and combine with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on aligning what is transferred to student capacity and task requirements, and best results typically come from hybrid, task-aware strategies that match distillation signals to model and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models or produce compact subnetworks via pruning and module replacement. The literature has grown into a design space of methods that transfer final outputs (soft logits), internal representations (feature maps, attention, layer activations), or training dynamics (curricula, evolving teachers), and which operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical and analytical work shows that success depends on matching the distilled information to student capacity and task demands, combining complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning or module replacement) when appropriate, and addressing practical constraints such as unlabeled-data needs, robustness transfer, and optimization stability. Effective distillation usually involves exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to the student, and selecting task-relevant knowledge rather than naively copying all teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central and Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a versatile and effective approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD’s strengths arise from its ability to transfer soft targets, internal representations, and task-relevant signals to reshape student training dynamics, and it admits many practical variants (multi-teacher, adversarial, curriculum, online/evolutionary, and progressive replacement). At the same time, structured pruning and module-replacement methods can be competitive or complementary when latency, data, or compute constraints dominate. Best practice is a toolbox mentality: choose what to transfer to match student capacity, adapt the teacher–student relationship during training, and combine distillation with pruning or curriculum strategies when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as an indispensable, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designers choose what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules) as required by deployment constraints, KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to the student and task, guarding against teacher–student mismatches, and addressing limits in robustness transfer and data/compute demands through hybrid and student-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. The literature provides many complementary distillation objectives and workflows — soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effectiveness depends strongly on teacher–student capacity gaps, the exact form of transferred information, task characteristics, and data availability; best practice is to select or adapt distillation signals to the student and downstream task and to combine methods where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolbox — selecting which signals to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and hybridizing distillation with complementary compression methods — KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits (data and teacher–student mismatch, compute cost) and should be compared against or combined with pruning and simple baselines in constrained regimes.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a configurable toolbox of techniques chosen to match student capacity, task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical compression combines forms of transferred knowledge (logits, internal representations, attention/feature structure), teacher engineering (confidence- or task-aware weighting, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules), adversarial/robustness-aware objectives, and complementary compression such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. The recommended approach is to select and combine distillation components according to the specific application rather than relying on one canonical loss.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Complementary Tools and Task-Aware Strategies for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large neural models into efficient students while preserving performance. A growing literature demonstrates a wide array of KD formulations—response-based, feature-based, layer-wise, adversarial, progressive replacing, and online/evolutionary teacher strategies—each addressing specific limitations such as teacher-student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, adversarial vulnerability, data complexity, and continual learning. Distillation should be treated as a toolbox: methods must be chosen and combined according to task demands (e.g., NLP summarization, ranking, detection, or incremental learning) and practical constraints (data availability, latency, and robustness requirements). When combined with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering, distillation can achieve large speedups with small accuracy loss; in some settings simple shrink-and-fine-tune can also be competitive. Overall, effective compression requires matching the distillation technique to the target task and model constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.
