papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that reliably compresses large models into smaller, deployable students when signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task needs. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation), adversarial or contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and robustness. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute demands, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when and the selective use of complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label matching into a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and task-aware schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting or selecting teacher signals to be student-friendly, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require it. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, minimizing teacher–student mismatch, and reducing the data and compute overhead of effective distillation.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis

Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox: Central Role and Practical Limits in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applicable family of methods for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When treated as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox—selecting which teacher signals to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention or feature correlations), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a universal panacea: its effectiveness depends on task complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, availability of data, and the choice of transferred signals, and in some deployment regimes simpler compression-first strategies can be preferable. Practical adoption therefore requires careful teacher engineering, signal selection, and integration with other compression methods to balance accuracy, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the state of knowledge distillation (KD) and its role in model compression for deep learning and NLP. It surveys what is transferred from teachers to students (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive/evolving schemes), the principal mechanisms by which distillation benefits students (label smoothing, reduced data complexity, representation shaping, and gradient/decision-boundary effects), common applications across NLP tasks, empirical practicalities and trade-offs (teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness transfer, and compute/latency constraints), and recommended task-aware, hybrid practices that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. The synthesis also highlights recurring open challenges such as reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant teacher signals for a given student capacity, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, choosing suitable teacher schedules, and integrating complementary compression techniques when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that success depends less on a single canonical loss and more on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and adapted to the student and the target task. Best results arise when distillation methods (1) expose informative internal representations rather than only final logits, (2) adapt or curate teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and (3) combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement). When applied with attention to these aspects, distillation yields compact models that maintain high accuracy, can inherit robustness, and scale to practical inference budgets.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, diverse family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-logit matching into a toolbox that also transfers internal representations, attention and feature statistics, and training dynamics; it is used in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical work shows KD can deliver strong accuracy–latency–memory trade-offs across vision and many NLP tasks, but its success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement). Important open problems include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora or heavy distillation compute.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a model-agnostic technique to improve model quality while having a fixed capacity budget. It is a commonly used technique for model compression, where a larger capacity teacher model with better quality is used to train a more compact student model with better inference efficiency. Through distillation, one hopes to benefit from student's compactness, without sacrificing too much on model quality. Despite the large success of knowledge distillation, better understanding of how it benefits student model's training dynamics remains under-explored. In this paper, we categorize teacher's knowledge into three hierarchical levels and study its effects on knowledge distillation: (1) knowledge of the `universe', where KD brings a regularization effect through label smoothing; (2) domain knowledge, where teacher injects class relationships prior to student's logit layer geometry; and (3) instance specific knowledge, where teacher rescales student model's per-instance gradients based on its measurement on the event difficulty. Using systematic analyses and extensive empirical studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we confirm that the aforementioned three factors play a major role in knowledge distillation. Furthermore, based on our findings, we diagnose some of the failure cases of applying KD from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher training, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals and teacher strategies to student capacity, task requirements, and available data; when designed carefully, KD enables substantial latency and memory gains while retaining strong accuracy across vision, NLP, ranking, retrieval, and reinforcement-learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: The Continuing Value of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (and When Hybrids Are Better)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained environments. KD works through multiple mechanisms — smoothing/regularization, transfer of structured class- and instance-level information, and alignment of internal representations — and can be improved by task-aware, teacher-aware, and curriculum-inspired strategies. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: structured pruning and module-replacement methods can match or exceed KD under certain data- or compute-constrained regimes, and simple strategies like shrink-and-fine-tune sometimes outperform explicit distillation for particular pre-trained NLP models and datasets. Best outcomes typically come from principled combinations: selecting or training student-friendly teachers, matching intermediate representations selectively, using task-aware filters, and combining KD with pruning or specialized distillation objectives tailored to the model and task.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Complementary Tools and Task-Aware Strategies for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large neural models into efficient students while preserving performance. A growing literature demonstrates a wide array of KD formulations—response-based, feature-based, layer-wise, adversarial, progressive replacing, and online/evolutionary teacher strategies—each addressing specific limitations such as teacher-student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, adversarial vulnerability, data complexity, and continual learning. Distillation should be treated as a toolbox: methods must be chosen and combined according to task demands (e.g., NLP summarization, ranking, detection, or incremental learning) and practical constraints (data availability, latency, and robustness requirements). When combined with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering, distillation can achieve large speedups with small accuracy loss; in some settings simple shrink-and-fine-tune can also be competitive. Overall, effective compression requires matching the distillation technique to the target task and model constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: On Learning the Geodesic Path for Incremental Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Neural networks notoriously suffer from the problem of catastrophic forgetting, the phenomenon of forgetting the past knowledge when acquiring new knowledge. Overcoming catastrophic forgetting is of significant importance to emulate the process of "incremental learning", where the model is capable of learning from sequential experience in an efficient and robust way. State-of-the-art techniques for incremental learning make use of knowledge distillation towards preventing catastrophic forgetting. Therein, one updates the network while ensuring that the network's responses to previously seen concepts remain stable throughout updates. This in practice is done by minimizing the dissimilarity between current and previous responses of the network one way or another. Our work contributes a novel method to the arsenal of distillation techniques. In contrast to the previous state of the art, we propose to firstly construct low-dimensional manifolds for previous and current responses and minimize the dissimilarity between the responses along the geodesic connecting the manifolds. This induces a more formidable knowledge distillation with smooth properties which preserves the past knowledge more efficiently as observed by our comprehensive empirical study.

Practical success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, task characteristics, and available data.

Success requires matching what is transferred to the student and the task, using multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and guarding against mismatches or unnecessary constraints imposed by poorly chosen teacher signals.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox. papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, and feature correlations, and extend to adversarial, contrastive, curriculum, multi-teacher, and meta-learned strategies. Best practices emphasize selecting which teacher signals to transfer, matching distilled information to student capacity and task needs, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning shows that task-aware, hybrid distillation pipelines typically deliver the most reliable trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. KD succeeds not because it is a single fixed recipe but because it is a design space: practitioners can choose what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, feature correlations, or decision-boundary information), how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and whether to combine distillation with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. KD yields consistent gains when matched to task constraints and student capacity, but it has limits — notably sensitivity to teacher–student gaps, data complexity, and some robustness-transfer failures — that motivate hybrid, task-aware strategies and careful teacher engineering.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Structured Pruning Learns Compact and Accurate Models
papers_seen.abstract: The growing size of neural language models has led to increased attention in model compression. The two predominant approaches are pruning, which gradually removes weights from a pre-trained model, and distillation, which trains a smaller compact model to match a larger one. Pruning methods can significantly reduce the model size but hardly achieve large speedups as distillation. However, distillation methods require large amounts of unlabeled data and are expensive to train. In this work, we propose a task-specific structured pruning method CoFi (Coarse- and Fine-grained Pruning), which delivers highly parallelizable subnetworks and matches the distillation methods in both accuracy and latency, without resorting to any unlabeled data. Our key insight is to jointly prune coarse-grained (e.g., layers) and fine-grained (e.g., heads and hidden units) modules, which controls the pruning decision of each parameter with masks of different granularity. We also devise a layerwise distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from unpruned to pruned models during optimization. Our experiments on GLUE and SQuAD datasets show that CoFi yields models with over 10x speedups with a small accuracy drop, showing its effectiveness and efficiency compared to previous pruning and distillation approaches.

Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Improving Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: This paper explores the use of knowledge distillation to improve a Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) (Liu et al., 2019) for learning text representations across multiple natural language understanding tasks. Although ensemble learning can improve model performance, serving an ensemble of large DNNs such as MT-DNN can be prohibitively expensive. Here we apply the knowledge distillation method (Hinton et al., 2015) in the multi-task learning setting. For each task, we train an ensemble of different MT-DNNs (teacher) that outperforms any single model, and then train a single MT-DNN (student) via multi-task learning to \emph{distill} knowledge from these ensemble teachers. We show that the distilled MT-DNN significantly outperforms the original MT-DNN on 7 out of 9 GLUE tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark (single model) to 83.7\% (1.5\% absolute improvement\footnote{ Based on the GLUE leaderboard at https://gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard as of April 1, 2019.}). The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/namisan/mt-dnn.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring the behavior and internal structure of large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-label matching into a broad design space that includes logits transfer, layer- and feature-wise alignment, attention or correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement. Practical success is task- and capacity-aware: practitioners must choose what to transfer, adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and often combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, module replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance in many vision and NLP tasks, its effectiveness depends on data complexity, teacher–student gaps, and the choice of transferred signals, and alternative or hybrid pipelines can be preferable in some regimes.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Model Compression — Best Practice Is a Hybrid, Task-aware Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) continues to be one of the most effective approaches to produce compact, high-performing models for deep learning and NLP. However, KD is not a single recipe: its strengths (soft-target transfer, ensemble compression, and the ability to reshape student training dynamics) come with practical costs and failure modes. Recent work shows structured pruning and alternative compression strategies can match or exceed KD on latency or data-efficiency in some settings. I argue that the best practical path is hybrid: combine KD with task-aware layer-wise methods, internal-representation matching, and targeted robustness or pruning techniques, and choose specific flavors (e.g., multi-teacher, adversarial, progressive replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) according to task constraints and available data. The result is compact models that retain accuracy, generalization, and robustness without unnecessary computation or unlabeled-data requirements.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a broad design space for transferring predictive behavior from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Methods range from soft-target matching to internal-representation alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or task-aware filtering. Empirical evidence across natural language tasks (classification, summarization, translation, retrieval) and other domains shows that KD can preserve or approach teacher performance while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, data complexity, and task constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Practical Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When applied as a toolbox — combining soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation alignment, teacher engineering, adversarial or robustness-aware objectives, and, when appropriate, structured pruning or progressive module replacement — distillation routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while improving latency and memory. Its success depends on matching methods to the teacher–student capacity gap, task demands, and data availability; in some deployment regimes simpler compress-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies can be competitive. I argue that practitioners should treat distillation as a configurable set of techniques chosen to fit task constraints rather than a single off‑the‑shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as an indispensable, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designers choose what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules) as required by deployment constraints, KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to the student and task, guarding against teacher–student mismatches, and addressing limits in robustness transfer and data/compute demands through hybrid and student-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a rich set of methods to transfer information from larger "teacher" models to smaller "student" models or to produce compact models via pruning and module replacement. Approaches vary from matching soft targets to aligning internal representations, using adversarial objectives, contrastive or Wasserstein-based objectives, layer-wise and task-aware filters, and online or evolutionary teacher schedules. These techniques have been applied across domains including natural language understanding, summarization, machine translation, ranking, vision tasks, reinforcement learning, and incremental learning. Empirical work highlights that the benefits of distillation depend on teacher-student capacity gaps, what kind of knowledge is transferred (global label structure, domain priors, instance-specific signals), and data complexity; combining distillation with structured pruning or careful teacher selection often yields practical gains in latency and storage while preserving accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has evolved from a simple teacher-to-student soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox for producing compact, deployable models. Modern distillation methods transfer a variety of signals — logits, intermediate representations, attention and feature correlations, decision-boundary information, and training dynamics — and are commonly combined with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, adapting teacher behavior or selection over training, and using confidence- or task-aware weighting. While distillation routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP, important challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and managing teacher–student mismatch and data requirements.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategies for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, but its success hinges on matching the distillation strategy to task demands, student capacity, and data constraints. Rather than a single recipe, KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox combining soft-labels, internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, layer-wise filtering, adversarial objectives, and pruning or module-replacement where appropriate. When chosen and combined thoughtfully—exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and using task-aware selection—KD yields compact models that retain high performance, robustness, and practical latency gains.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring useful predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to smaller students. The field encompasses a wide spectrum of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher strategies, and combinations with structured pruning — each suited to different capacity gaps, data regimes, latency constraints, and robustness needs. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation helps by smoothing supervision, reducing data complexity, shaping per-instance gradients and decision boundaries, and providing representational priors that smaller models can exploit. Effective compression typically requires choosing or adapting what is transferred to the student's capacity and the target task, and often benefits from hybrid strategies (e.g., distillation plus pruning or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring behavioral and representational information from large teacher models to smaller student models so they meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, robustness) while preserving performance. KD has grown from soft-target matching into a rich, task-aware toolbox that includes logits and intermediate-representation matching, attention and feature-correlation transfer, self- and multi-teacher schemes, curriculum/meta-learning schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Key practical challenges include matching transferred signals to student capacity, bridging teacher–student gaps, managing data and robustness constraints, and choosing complementary compression steps for target deployment.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a model-agnostic technique to improve model quality while having a fixed capacity budget. It is a commonly used technique for model compression, where a larger capacity teacher model with better quality is used to train a more compact student model with better inference efficiency. Through distillation, one hopes to benefit from student's compactness, without sacrificing too much on model quality. Despite the large success of knowledge distillation, better understanding of how it benefits student model's training dynamics remains under-explored. In this paper, we categorize teacher's knowledge into three hierarchical levels and study its effects on knowledge distillation: (1) knowledge of the `universe', where KD brings a regularization effect through label smoothing; (2) domain knowledge, where teacher injects class relationships prior to student's logit layer geometry; and (3) instance specific knowledge, where teacher rescales student model's per-instance gradients based on its measurement on the event difficulty. Using systematic analyses and extensive empirical studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we confirm that the aforementioned three factors play a major role in knowledge distillation. Furthermore, based on our findings, we diagnose some of the failure cases of applying KD from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond soft-label supervision into a design space that includes intermediate-representation matching, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary teachers, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves compact model performance across vision and NLP tasks (including pretrained transformer compression, machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, and continual learning), but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity gap, availability of data, and task-specific constraints. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD's strength derives from a flexible design space — transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations, and decision-boundary information — and from compatibility with complementary strategies such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and teacher adaptation. While KD does not universally dominate every setting, when applied in a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware way it reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while delivering practical latency, memory, and robustness benefits.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that reliably compresses large models into smaller, deployable students when signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task needs. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation), adversarial or contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and robustness. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute demands, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when and the selective use of complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: An Argument for Its Central Role in Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students when treated as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox. By selecting and combining signals (soft outputs, internal representations, attention/feature maps), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and integrating distillation with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules), practitioners can achieve strong accuracy–latency–size trade-offs. KD has limits — including teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute needs, and uneven robustness transfer — so it must be applied judiciously and compared or combined with other compression approaches in constrained regimes.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching into a rich design space that includes logits and temperature tuning, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and progressive module-replacement pipelines. Empirical work across computer vision, language understanding, translation, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD often substantially narrows the performance gap between teacher and student while improving latency and memory usage; however, success depends on matching what and how information is transferred to student capacity, task constraints, and available data. Complementary methods (structured pruning, module replacement, and teacher adaptation) and task-aware choices usually yield the most reliable compression outcomes. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, handling teacher–student capacity gaps, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that, when designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and combined with complementary compression techniques, routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. Its mechanisms include soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation matching, teacher scheduling (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), and adversarial or contrastive objectives. Practical success requires adapting teacher signals to task and data constraints and recognizing limitations such as teacher–student capacity gaps, data requirements, and robustness transfer challenges.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into compact, deployable ones. When applied thoughtfully — by distilling internal representations, aligning intermediate layers in a task-aware way, optimizing teacher dynamics, and using distributional or adversarial objectives — distillation can deliver accuracy, latency, and robustness gains across vision, ranking, and NLP tasks. Distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a toolkit: combine representation-level transfer, teacher engineering (including learned or evolving teachers), multi-teacher confidence weighting, and targeted adversarial or contrastive objectives. In some settings structured pruning or simple shrink-and-fine-tune strategies are competitive, so practitioners should match the distillation strategy to data availability, task complexity, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in both vision and natural language processing. The field has expanded well beyond soft-target matching to include representation-level alignment, attention and correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, progressive module replacement, and hybrids that pair distillation with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering. Effective compression is task- and capacity-aware: choosing what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student constraints is key to preserving accuracy, latency, and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.
