papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Structured Pruning Learns Compact and Accurate Models
papers_seen.abstract: The growing size of neural language models has led to increased attention in model compression. The two predominant approaches are pruning, which gradually removes weights from a pre-trained model, and distillation, which trains a smaller compact model to match a larger one. Pruning methods can significantly reduce the model size but hardly achieve large speedups as distillation. However, distillation methods require large amounts of unlabeled data and are expensive to train. In this work, we propose a task-specific structured pruning method CoFi (Coarse- and Fine-grained Pruning), which delivers highly parallelizable subnetworks and matches the distillation methods in both accuracy and latency, without resorting to any unlabeled data. Our key insight is to jointly prune coarse-grained (e.g., layers) and fine-grained (e.g., heads and hidden units) modules, which controls the pruning decision of each parameter with masks of different granularity. We also devise a layerwise distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from unpruned to pruned models during optimization. Our experiments on GLUE and SQuAD datasets show that CoFi yields models with over 10x speedups with a small accuracy drop, showing its effectiveness and efficiency compared to previous pruning and distillation approaches.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) condenses information from larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, more efficient models to enable deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade this basic teacher–student framework has diversified: methods transfer logits, hidden/internal representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or policy behavior; teachers may be fixed, jointly trained, or evolved; distillation objectives may use soft-label matching, contrastive or distributional distances, adversarial losses, or curriculum-based schedules. Empirical work demonstrates KD improves compact model performance across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and reinforcement learning, and recent advances target robustness, task-aware filtering, multi-teacher selection, and compression without large unlabeled data. Despite practical successes, open issues remain in choosing what to transfer, matching capacity to distilled data complexity, and reliably transferring robustness and decision-boundary information.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching into a rich design space that includes logits and temperature tuning, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and progressive module-replacement pipelines. Empirical work across computer vision, language understanding, translation, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD often substantially narrows the performance gap between teacher and student while improving latency and memory usage; however, success depends on matching what and how information is transferred to student capacity, task constraints, and available data. Complementary methods (structured pruning, module replacement, and teacher adaptation) and task-aware choices usually yield the most reliable compression outcomes. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, handling teacher–student capacity gaps, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most usefully viewed not as a single algorithm but as a configurable, task-aware toolbox. When practitioners select what to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits — it depends on data complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the choice of transferred signals — and in some regimes alternative compression strategies can match or exceed distillation unless hybridized thoughtfully.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and flexible family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The literature treats KD as a design space rather than a single recipe: practitioners transfer soft logits, internal representations, attention/feature statistics, or training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, or self-distillation schedules; and they often combine KD with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective distillation aligns the form and amount of transferred information with student capacity and task needs, and best practice is task-aware, hybrid, and selective about what to copy from the teacher.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space rather than a single algorithm. By transferring behavioral and representational signals from larger teachers to smaller students, KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. When carefully matched to student capacity and task constraints — and when combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, confidence weighting, and targeted representation transfer — KD yields practical, deployable models with strong accuracy–latency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers
papers_seen.abstract: We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. Practical compression succeeds by (1) exposing and aligning informative internal representations, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task requirements, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. With these design patterns, distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world deployment constraints, though limits remain when data is scarce or teacher–student gaps are large.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware, and hybrid set of techniques for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors, and by combining these signals with teacher engineering and complementary compression methods. While KD often yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its effectiveness depends on student capacity, task characteristics, data availability, and careful selection or adaptation of teacher signals.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Task-Aware Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger models (teachers) into smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency. The literature has expanded from simple soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, progressive module replacement, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or module replacement. Empirical and analytic work shows that effectiveness depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, the target task, and available data; combining complementary compression tools often yields the best practical trade-offs. Open challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, reliable transfer of robustness, and minimizing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox. Practical compression succeeds when designers choose which teacher signals to transfer (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or feature statistics), adapt or engineer teachers to student capacity (single, multi-, evolving, or student-friendly teachers), and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and improve latency and memory, open challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox that, when matched to student capacity and combined with complementary compression strategies, produces compact models that approach the performance of large teachers while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective use of distillation emphasizes representation-level signals, teacher adaptation, and selective or progressive transfer of modules; its limits arise from teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute availability, and the choice of which form of knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its strengths arise from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, internal representation transfer, teacher engineering, and supervised schedules), and the most reliable practical strategies treat KD as a configurable toolbox that is combined with pruning or module replacement when deployment constraints demand it. Practitioners obtain the best trade-offs by matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics to the task, and using hybrid pipelines tailored to data, latency, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond soft-label supervision into a design space that includes intermediate-representation matching, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary teachers, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves compact model performance across vision and NLP tasks (including pretrained transformer compression, machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, and continual learning), but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity gap, availability of data, and task-specific constraints. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: Essential, Effective, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single soft-label trick into a broad, task-aware toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into compact, deployable students. When matched to student capacity, adapted to task constraints, and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement), KD routinely produces models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness needs. At the same time, KD has limits tied to data requirements, teacher–student capacity gaps, and robustness transfer; practical deployment benefits from hybrid, selective, and teacher-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and versatile approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students in vision and NLP. KD is best treated as a configurable, task-aware toolbox that transfers logits, internal representations, attention or feature structure, and can be combined with teacher engineering, multi-teacher or online schedules, adversarial/contrastive objectives, and complementary compression such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness; however, limits remain related to teacher–student capacity gaps, data requirements, and reliable robustness transfer. Practical success comes from task-aware selection of signals, adaptive teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that incorporate pruning or module replacement when necessary.

The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Evolving, and Complementary to Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into compact students suitable for deployment. A broad and active literature has developed specialized KD variants that address teacher selection, internal representation transfer, robustness, task-specific filtering, online and ensemble distillation, and model-structure-aware compression. While KD is highly effective across vision and NLP tasks, recent work shows that pruning and module-replacement strategies can be competitive or complementary, particularly when unlabeled data or heavy distillation training is impractical. Best practice is to treat distillation as a toolbox: select methods that reduce teacher-student capacity gap, transfer internal representations and task-relevant features, and incorporate confidence or robustness objectives when needed, while considering pruning or progressive replacement when latency or data constraints dominate.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond soft‑target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes logits and soft-label matching, intermediate-representation and attention/feature matching, inter-channel and feature-correlation objectives, adversarial and contrastive losses, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self- and meta-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results show KD routinely improves compact-model performance across vision, language, ranking, generation, and reinforcement learning when its components are chosen to match student capacity, task constraints, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing data and compute costs of distillation, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models or produce compact subnetworks via pruning and module replacement. The literature has grown into a design space of methods that transfer final outputs (soft logits), internal representations (feature maps, attention, layer activations), or training dynamics (curricula, evolving teachers), and which operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical and analytical work shows that success depends on matching the distilled information to student capacity and task demands, combining complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning or module replacement) when appropriate, and addressing practical constraints such as unlabeled-data needs, robustness transfer, and optimization stability. Effective distillation usually involves exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to the student, and selecting task-relevant knowledge rather than naively copying all teacher behavior.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. The literature provides many complementary distillation objectives and workflows — soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effectiveness depends strongly on teacher–student capacity gaps, the exact form of transferred information, task characteristics, and data availability; best practice is to select or adapt distillation signals to the student and downstream task and to combine methods where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that success depends less on a single canonical loss and more on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and adapted to the student and the target task. Best results arise when distillation methods (1) expose informative internal representations rather than only final logits, (2) adapt or curate teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and (3) combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement). When applied with attention to these aspects, distillation yields compact models that maintain high accuracy, can inherit robustness, and scale to practical inference budgets.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates predictive behavior from large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster models for deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and evolutionary teachers, confidence-weighted and task-aware strategies, and integrations with pruning or module-replacement. Across vision and NLP tasks these methods enable substantial reductions in parameters and latency while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance, though success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, selecting or adapting teachers, and addressing data and robustness constraints. Practical best practice is to select and combine KD variants according to task demands and resource constraints rather than rely on a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Complementary Tools and Task-Aware Strategies for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large neural models into efficient students while preserving performance. A growing literature demonstrates a wide array of KD formulations—response-based, feature-based, layer-wise, adversarial, progressive replacing, and online/evolutionary teacher strategies—each addressing specific limitations such as teacher-student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, adversarial vulnerability, data complexity, and continual learning. Distillation should be treated as a toolbox: methods must be chosen and combined according to task demands (e.g., NLP summarization, ranking, detection, or incremental learning) and practical constraints (data availability, latency, and robustness requirements). When combined with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering, distillation can achieve large speedups with small accuracy loss; in some settings simple shrink-and-fine-tune can also be competitive. Overall, effective compression requires matching the distillation technique to the target task and model constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Towards Effective and Robust Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Distillation-Centric Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically powerful tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students. I argue that the most reliable path to high-quality compressed models in both vision and NLP is a hybrid approach that (1) emphasizes internal-representation and layer-wise distillation for transferring structured task-relevant knowledge, (2) uses task-aware selection and teacher-selection strategies to reduce irrelevant signal, (3) integrates adversarial and robustness-aware techniques when robustness matters, and (4) combines distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement when latency and memory constraints dominate. This position synthesizes empirical and theoretical findings across distillation, multi-teacher strategies, robustness, and pruning to recommend practical design patterns for model compression.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.
