                    Topic: Knowledge distillation or model compression in deep learning or NLP

                    Articles:
                    [{'author': 'Diaz', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.'}, {'author': 'Lee', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a diverse set of approaches that transfer logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics; employ single, multi-, or evolving-teacher schedules; and combine naturally with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When practitioners match what is transferred to student capacity and the target task, distillation commonly yields compact models with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs; remaining challenges include capacity gaps, robustness transfer, data requirements, and selecting task-relevant internal signals.'}, {'author': 'Tucker', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood and applied as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Effective compression requires choosing which signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, decision-boundary cues), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity (including online or evolving teachers and student-friendly teacher training), and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) when deployment constraints demand it. Across vision, NLP, machine translation, and reinforcement learning, this hybrid, capacity-matched approach consistently yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements.'}, {'author': 'Adams', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.'}, {'author': 'Calderon', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.'}, {'author': 'Davidson', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.'}, {'author': 'Morgan', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow technique for transferring soft labels into a broad, pragmatic design space that produces compact, deployable models in vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning. KD’s strengths arise from multiple complementary transfer mechanisms (logits, hidden states, attention/feature structure, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, progressive module replacement, and curriculum or teacher-scheduling strategies). Practical success requires task-aware decisions about which signals to transfer, careful handling of teacher–student capacity gaps, and hybrid pipelines that match data, latency, and robustness constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when applied thoughtfully, remaining challenges include reliable robustness transfer, dependence on data and compute for some pipelines, and principled selection of task-relevant intermediate signals.'}, {'author': 'Ryan', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.'}, {'author': 'Mcclain', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.'}, {'author': 'Bush', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned teachers, multi-teacher or online schemes), and task-specific constraints. When combined with complementary approaches such as structured pruning or curriculum-style supervision, distillation yields compact models suitable for real-world NLP and vision deployments while enabling trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness.'}, {'author': 'Bowman', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring information from a teacher to a smaller student. Methods vary widely: matching output soft-labels, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and contrastive approaches, curriculum and meta-learning strategies, and task-aware layer selection. In NLP, and particularly with large pretrained Transformers, distillation is applied both during pretraining and fine-tuning; alternative compression strategies (e.g., pruning) are often combined with distillation to trade off size, speed, and accuracy. Empirical and theoretical work highlights multiple mechanisms by which distillation helps students, including regularization, reduced data complexity, and per-instance gradient shaping.'}, {'author': 'Heath', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP the field has moved beyond single-loss soft-target matching to a rich set of transferable signals and training schedules that include logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, confidence-aware weighting, multi- or online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred knowledge to student capacity and task constraints, adaptively shaping teacher signals, and—when needed—integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, dealing with teacher–student capacity gaps, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.'}, {'author': 'Gardner', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation', 'abstract': 'Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.'}, {'author': 'Kim', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designed to match what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), how teachers and students are coupled (teacher engineering, online or multi-teacher schemes, curriculum or route-based schedules), and when combined with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement), KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness requirements. However, the practical success of KD depends on matching transfer signals to student capacity and task demands, managing teacher–student capacity gaps, and addressing data and robustness constraints; in some settings, alternative or hybrid compression strategies may be preferable.'}, {'author': 'Brown', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the last decade the field has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, contrastive and adversarial objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical application is task- and capacity-aware: success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and data availability, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools where appropriate.'}, {'author': 'Santos', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.'}, {'author': 'Arroyo', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Work across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding shows KD variants — from soft-label matching to internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, adversarial and curriculum-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines combining pruning or module replacement — routinely recover much of teacher performance when the distillation strategy is matched to task demands and student capacity. Important limitations remain: sensitivity to teacher–student capacity gaps, reliance on unlabeled data and heavy distillation compute in some pipelines, and uneven transfer of robustness, motivating continued research into targeted transfer signals and efficient, student-aware distillation protocols.'}, {'author': 'Lee', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Empirical Findings, and Best Practices', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a broad set of techniques that include representation-level matching, multi- and online-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning and progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, natural language understanding, summarization, machine translation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD can substantially close the gap between compact students and their larger teachers, but success depends on matching the form and amount of transferred knowledge to student capacity, task demands, and data/latency/robustness constraints.'}, {'author': 'Liu', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.'}, {'author': 'Shaffer', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation', 'abstract': 'The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.'}, {'author': 'Peterson', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers', 'abstract': "We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower."}, {'author': 'Hernandez', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.'}, {'author': 'Ross', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.'}, {'author': 'Blair', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection', 'abstract': 'Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.'}, {'author': 'Duncan', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises a toolbox of techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, engineering teacher supervision to be student-friendly, and choosing complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require them. While KD is often indispensable for deployment, alternative or hybrid strategies (structured pruning, shrink-and-fine-tune) can be competitive in constrained regimes.'}, {'author': 'Owens', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: Indispensable but Context-Dependent', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space of transferable signals (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics), teacher–student coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, progressive replacement, and student-friendly teacher design), and complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement). KD can often recover much of the teacher’s performance while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on task constraints, student capacity, data availability, and attention to robustness. The best practical posture is to treat KD as a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware toolbox and to combine distillation with other compression methods when deployment constraints demand it.'}, {'author': 'Mckay', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, diverse family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-logit matching into a toolbox that also transfers internal representations, attention and feature statistics, and training dynamics; it is used in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical work shows KD can deliver strong accuracy–latency–memory trade-offs across vision and many NLP tasks, but its success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement). Important open problems include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora or heavy distillation compute.'}, {'author': 'Adams', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, Task Considerations, and Best Practices', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple soft-target matching into a rich set of methods that transfer logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information; use single, multiple, evolving, or learned teachers; and combine with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on aligning what is transferred to student capacity and task requirements, and best results typically come from hybrid, task-aware strategies that match distillation signals to model and deployment constraints.'}, {'author': 'Fowler', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression', 'abstract': "Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation."}, {'author': 'Perez', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that reliably compresses large models into smaller, deployable students when signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task needs. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation), adversarial or contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and robustness. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute demands, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when and the selective use of complementary compression strategies.'}]

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning tasks, KD methods have been extended with architectural, training, and curriculum innovations to address capacity gaps, robustness, and task specificity. Effective deployment of KD requires matching what is distilled (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or structural operators) to the student capacity and the target task; complementary methods such as structured pruning and curriculum-based teacher schedules can further improve trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Towards Effective and Robust Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Distillation-Centric Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically powerful tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students. I argue that the most reliable path to high-quality compressed models in both vision and NLP is a hybrid approach that (1) emphasizes internal-representation and layer-wise distillation for transferring structured task-relevant knowledge, (2) uses task-aware selection and teacher-selection strategies to reduce irrelevant signal, (3) integrates adversarial and robustness-aware techniques when robustness matters, and (4) combines distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement when latency and memory constraints dominate. This position synthesizes empirical and theoretical findings across distillation, multi-teacher strategies, robustness, and pruning to recommend practical design patterns for model compression.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that reliably compresses large models into smaller, deployable students when signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task needs. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation), adversarial or contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and robustness. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute demands, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when and the selective use of complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) condenses information from larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, more efficient models to enable deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade this basic teacher–student framework has diversified: methods transfer logits, hidden/internal representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or policy behavior; teachers may be fixed, jointly trained, or evolved; distillation objectives may use soft-label matching, contrastive or distributional distances, adversarial losses, or curriculum-based schedules. Empirical work demonstrates KD improves compact model performance across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and reinforcement learning, and recent advances target robustness, task-aware filtering, multi-teacher selection, and compression without large unlabeled data. Despite practical successes, open issues remain in choosing what to transfer, matching capacity to distilled data complexity, and reliably transferring robustness and decision-boundary information.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into compact, deployable ones. When applied thoughtfully — by distilling internal representations, aligning intermediate layers in a task-aware way, optimizing teacher dynamics, and using distributional or adversarial objectives — distillation can deliver accuracy, latency, and robustness gains across vision, ranking, and NLP tasks. Distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a toolkit: combine representation-level transfer, teacher engineering (including learned or evolving teachers), multi-teacher confidence weighting, and targeted adversarial or contrastive objectives. In some settings structured pruning or simple shrink-and-fine-tune strategies are competitive, so practitioners should match the distillation strategy to data availability, task complexity, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Work across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding shows KD variants — from soft-label matching to internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, adversarial and curriculum-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines combining pruning or module replacement — routinely recover much of teacher performance when the distillation strategy is matched to task demands and student capacity. Important limitations remain: sensitivity to teacher–student capacity gaps, reliance on unlabeled data and heavy distillation compute in some pipelines, and uneven transfer of robustness, motivating continued research into targeted transfer signals and efficient, student-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox. Practical compression succeeds when designers choose which teacher signals to transfer (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or feature statistics), adapt or engineer teachers to student capacity (single, multi-, evolving, or student-friendly teachers), and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and improve latency and memory, open challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a large, well-developed design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, faster students or compact subnetworks. The literature documents many complementary approaches — soft-target matching, intermediate representation alignment, layer- and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schedules, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines — and evaluates them across NLP, machine translation, summarization, retrieval, vision, and sequential decision tasks. Practical success depends on choosing what to transfer, how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task needs, and how to combine distillation with pruning or module replacement to meet latency and robustness constraints. Ongoing challenges highlight the need for task-aware representational targets, student-friendly teacher design, and methods that avoid heavy reliance on large unlabeled corpora while preserving robustness and efficient inference.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. Practical compression succeeds by (1) exposing and aligning informative internal representations, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task requirements, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. With these design patterns, distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world deployment constraints, though limits remain when data is scarce or teacher–student gaps are large.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting and combining appropriate distilled signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention/feature statistics), adapting or engineering teachers to student capacity, and integrating complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules), practitioners can produce compact models that retain high accuracy and practical latency. Success requires matching what is transferred to the student and the task, using multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and guarding against mismatches or unnecessary constraints imposed by poorly chosen teacher signals.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned teachers, multi-teacher or online schemes), and task-specific constraints. When combined with complementary approaches such as structured pruning or curriculum-style supervision, distillation yields compact models suitable for real-world NLP and vision deployments while enabling trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label matching into a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and task-aware schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting or selecting teacher signals to be student-friendly, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require it. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, minimizing teacher–student mismatch, and reducing the data and compute overhead of effective distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond soft‑target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes logits and soft-label matching, intermediate-representation and attention/feature matching, inter-channel and feature-correlation objectives, adversarial and contrastive losses, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self- and meta-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results show KD routinely improves compact-model performance across vision, language, ranking, generation, and reinforcement learning when its components are chosen to match student capacity, task constraints, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing data and compute costs of distillation, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. The literature provides many complementary distillation objectives and workflows — soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effectiveness depends strongly on teacher–student capacity gaps, the exact form of transferred information, task characteristics, and data availability; best practice is to select or adapt distillation signals to the student and downstream task and to combine methods where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), practitioners can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective compression requires matching distillation strategies to task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints; blindly applying a single distillation recipe risks wasted effort or suboptimal trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching into a rich design space that includes logits and temperature tuning, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and progressive module-replacement pipelines. Empirical work across computer vision, language understanding, translation, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows KD often substantially narrows the performance gap between teacher and student while improving latency and memory usage; however, success depends on matching what and how information is transferred to student capacity, task constraints, and available data. Complementary methods (structured pruning, module replacement, and teacher adaptation) and task-aware choices usually yield the most reliable compression outcomes. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, handling teacher–student capacity gaps, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques aim to transfer performance from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, more efficient models for deployment or specialized use. Approaches span logit-based soft-label distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, teacher design and selection strategies, online/evolutionary teachers, curriculum or route-based supervision, and combinations with pruning and adversarial methods. In NLP, distillation has been adapted to pretrained transformers via progressive module replacement, layer-wise and task-aware filters, and by leveraging distilled data (pseudo-labeling) or parameter shrinking. Trade-offs include reliance on unlabeled data, teacher-student capacity gaps, and robustness concerns; recent work addresses these via teacher adaptation, confidence-weighting, and distillation objectives targeting representation geometry and decision boundaries.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, effective distillation is a design space of complementary techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher design, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or progressive module replacement. When chosen and combined with attention to teacher–student capacity, task characteristics, and data availability, distillation reliably yields compact models that preserve accuracy and can transfer robustness; when misapplied it can be outperformed by simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or structured pruning strategies. I argue that the best practical posture is to treat distillation as a task-aware hybrid toolbox: prioritize representation-level transfer and teacher engineering, use confidence- or task-aware weighting for multiple signals, integrate robustness-aware objectives when needed, and combine distillation with pruning or module replacement when latency/memory constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models. It works through multiple mechanisms — soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, and structured guidance — and can be adapted via curriculum strategies, multi-teacher weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary-aware examples, and progressive module replacement. Distillation often yields models that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distillation methods to task properties and model capacity; in some settings structured pruning or hybrid approaches can match or exceed distillation without the need for large unlabeled corpora. I argue that distillation is indispensable for practical NLP and deep learning deployments when used with task-aware, representation-level, and teacher-aware strategies, and that combining distillation with complementary compression methods yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.
