papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Model Compression — Best Practice Is a Hybrid, Task-aware Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) continues to be one of the most effective approaches to produce compact, high-performing models for deep learning and NLP. However, KD is not a single recipe: its strengths (soft-target transfer, ensemble compression, and the ability to reshape student training dynamics) come with practical costs and failure modes. Recent work shows structured pruning and alternative compression strategies can match or exceed KD on latency or data-efficiency in some settings. I argue that the best practical path is hybrid: combine KD with task-aware layer-wise methods, internal-representation matching, and targeted robustness or pruning techniques, and choose specific flavors (e.g., multi-teacher, adversarial, progressive replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) according to task constraints and available data. The result is compact models that retain accuracy, generalization, and robustness without unnecessary computation or unlabeled-data requirements.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Evolving, and Complementary to Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into compact students suitable for deployment. A broad and active literature has developed specialized KD variants that address teacher selection, internal representation transfer, robustness, task-specific filtering, online and ensemble distillation, and model-structure-aware compression. While KD is highly effective across vision and NLP tasks, recent work shows that pruning and module-replacement strategies can be competitive or complementary, particularly when unlabeled data or heavy distillation training is impractical. Best practice is to treat distillation as a toolbox: select methods that reduce teacher-student capacity gap, transfer internal representations and task-relevant features, and incorporate confidence or robustness objectives when needed, while considering pruning or progressive replacement when latency or data constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, multifaceted approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching into a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-map matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher regimes, confidence-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity, adapting teacher supervision, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques when deployment constraints (latency, memory, robustness) demand it. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing dependence on large distillation datasets or compute, and principled selection of task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond soft-label supervision into a design space that includes intermediate-representation matching, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary teachers, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves compact model performance across vision and NLP tasks (including pretrained transformer compression, machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, and continual learning), but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity gap, availability of data, and task-specific constraints. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), practitioners can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective compression requires matching distillation strategies to task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints; blindly applying a single distillation recipe risks wasted effort or suboptimal trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood and applied as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Effective compression requires choosing which signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, decision-boundary cues), adapting teacher supervision to student capacity (including online or evolving teachers and student-friendly teacher training), and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) when deployment constraints demand it. Across vision, NLP, machine translation, and reinforcement learning, this hybrid, capacity-matched approach consistently yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label matching into a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and task-aware schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting or selecting teacher signals to be student-friendly, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness demands require it. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, minimizing teacher–student mismatch, and reducing the data and compute overhead of effective distillation.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that reliably compresses large models into smaller, deployable students when signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task needs. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation), adversarial or contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and robustness. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute demands, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when and the selective use of complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, Task Considerations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple soft-target matching into a rich set of methods that transfer logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information; use single, multiple, evolving, or learned teachers; and combine with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on aligning what is transferred to student capacity and task requirements, and best results typically come from hybrid, task-aware strategies that match distillation signals to model and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP the field has moved beyond single-loss soft-target matching to a rich set of transferable signals and training schedules that include logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, confidence-aware weighting, multi- or online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred knowledge to student capacity and task constraints, adaptively shaping teacher signals, and—when needed—integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, dealing with teacher–student capacity gaps, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and natural language processing. KD encompasses transferring final outputs (soft logits), intermediate and attention representations, and aspects of training dynamics, and is most effective when chosen and combined with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) to match student capacity and task constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its practical success depends on teacher–student matching, data availability, and attention to robustness; hybrid, task-aware pipelines and careful teacher engineering are therefore recommended.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its many variants—logit transfer, intermediate-representation matching, attention- and feature-based matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- or online-teachers, and curriculum-style schedules—provide different trade-offs among accuracy, latency, robustness, and data requirements. Rather than a single recipe, effective compression arises from selecting and combining KD methods to match student capacity and task constraints, often in combination with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or module replacement.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practically central approach for producing compact neural models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher training, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals and teacher strategies to student capacity, task requirements, and available data; when designed carefully, KD enables substantial latency and memory gains while retaining strong accuracy across vision, NLP, ranking, retrieval, and reinforcement-learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a diverse and practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large models (teachers) to smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency while preserving performance. The literature spans soft-target (logit) transfer, internal- and layer-wise representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online/evolving teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical results across vision and a wide range of NLP tasks (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, dense retrieval) show that no single recipe suffices: success depends on the choice of distilled signal, teacher–student capacity gap, task complexity, and data availability. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a toolbox of complementary methods whose components should be selected and combined according to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD encompasses soft-label matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, and progressive or hybrid compression pipelines; when matched to student capacity and task constraints and combined with complementary methods (e.g., pruning or module replacement) it yields strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and memory. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora or heavy distillation compute.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. Practical compression succeeds by (1) exposing and aligning informative internal representations, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task requirements, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. With these design patterns, distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world deployment constraints, though limits remain when data is scarce or teacher–student gaps are large.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as an indispensable, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designers choose what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules) as required by deployment constraints, KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to the student and task, guarding against teacher–student mismatches, and addressing limits in robustness transfer and data/compute demands through hybrid and student-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD's strength derives from a flexible design space — transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations, and decision-boundary information — and from compatibility with complementary strategies such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and teacher adaptation. While KD does not universally dominate every setting, when applied in a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware way it reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while delivering practical latency, memory, and robustness benefits.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Evolving, and Complementary to Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into compact students suitable for deployment. A broad and active literature has developed specialized KD variants that address teacher selection, internal representation transfer, robustness, task-specific filtering, online and ensemble distillation, and model-structure-aware compression. While KD is highly effective across vision and NLP tasks, recent work shows that pruning and module-replacement strategies can be competitive or complementary, particularly when unlabeled data or heavy distillation training is impractical. Best practice is to treat distillation as a toolbox: select methods that reduce teacher-student capacity gap, transfer internal representations and task-relevant features, and incorporate confidence or robustness objectives when needed, while considering pruning or progressive replacement when latency or data constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and flexible family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The literature treats KD as a design space rather than a single recipe: practitioners transfer soft logits, internal representations, attention/feature statistics, or training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, or self-distillation schedules; and they often combine KD with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective distillation aligns the form and amount of transferred information with student capacity and task needs, and best practice is task-aware, hybrid, and selective about what to copy from the teacher.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large pretrained models into smaller, more efficient models by transferring learned knowledge from teacher to student. A rich variety of techniques have been developed: matching soft targets, aligning intermediate and internal representations, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. These techniques have been applied across vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning tasks, and have been analyzed to explain when and why distillation helps. Empirical work shows distillation can reduce model size and preserve or improve performance, but effectiveness depends on the choice of teacher, the form of transferred knowledge, data complexity, and task-specific design choices.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a large, well-developed design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, faster students or compact subnetworks. The literature documents many complementary approaches — soft-target matching, intermediate representation alignment, layer- and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schedules, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines — and evaluates them across NLP, machine translation, summarization, retrieval, vision, and sequential decision tasks. Practical success depends on choosing what to transfer, how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task needs, and how to combine distillation with pruning or module replacement to meet latency and robustness constraints. Ongoing challenges highlight the need for task-aware representational targets, student-friendly teacher design, and methods that avoid heavy reliance on large unlabeled corpora while preserving robustness and efficient inference.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP the field has moved beyond single-loss soft-target matching to a rich set of transferable signals and training schedules that include logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, confidence-aware weighting, multi- or online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred knowledge to student capacity and task constraints, adaptively shaping teacher signals, and—when needed—integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, dealing with teacher–student capacity gaps, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Task-Aware Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger models (teachers) into smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency. The literature has expanded from simple soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, progressive module replacement, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or module replacement. Empirical and analytic work shows that effectiveness depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, the target task, and available data; combining complementary compression tools often yields the best practical trade-offs. Open challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, reliable transfer of robustness, and minimizing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and natural language processing. KD encompasses transferring final outputs (soft logits), intermediate and attention representations, and aspects of training dynamics, and is most effective when chosen and combined with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, curriculum schedules) to match student capacity and task constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its practical success depends on teacher–student matching, data availability, and attention to robustness; hybrid, task-aware pipelines and careful teacher engineering are therefore recommended.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-label (logit) matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher regimes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity and task constraints, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox that, when matched to student capacity and combined with complementary compression strategies, produces compact models that approach the performance of large teachers while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective use of distillation emphasizes representation-level signals, teacher adaptation, and selective or progressive transfer of modules; its limits arise from teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute availability, and the choice of which form of knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the last decade the field has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, contrastive and adversarial objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical application is task- and capacity-aware: success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and data availability, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: Indispensable but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space of transferable signals (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics), teacher–student coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, progressive replacement, and student-friendly teacher design), and complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement). KD can often recover much of the teacher’s performance while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on task constraints, student capacity, data availability, and attention to robustness. The best practical posture is to treat KD as a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware toolbox and to combine distillation with other compression methods when deployment constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, task-aware design space for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. The field has expanded from soft-label matching to include intermediate-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary and online teachers, and progressive module replacement. KD is most effective when chosen and combined according to task constraints, student capacity, data availability, and goals (latency, memory, or robustness); complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive replacement are often used alongside KD to meet deployment requirements. Empirical work shows that, when applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that recover much of teacher performance while delivering meaningful reductions in parameter count and inference cost, though open challenges remain around teacher–student gaps, robustness transfer, and data-limited regimes.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolkit for producing compact models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves student performance by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and training dynamics, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as part of a hybrid compression pipeline—selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when needed.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.
